title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
authors: Andrew J. Reagan, Lewis Mitchell, Dilan Kiley, Christopher M. Danforth, Peter Sheridan Dodds
key_findings: EPJ Data Science 5. Sentiment trajectories of Project Gutenberg fiction cluster into six core arcs (rags-to-riches rise, tragedy fall, man-in-a-hole fall-rise, Icarus rise-fall, Cinderella rise-fall-rise, Oedipus fall-rise-fall) as building blocks.
Some arcs associated with higher download counts.
Robustness via matrix decomposition, supervised and unsupervised learning.
practical_applications: Pick an arc shape deliberately per piece; 'man in a hole' (fall then rise) fits problem→solution content.
limitations: Text sentiment (word valence) only, not audience feelings; corpus size reported inconsistently (1,327 vs 1,737); downloads ≠ quality; arc names here from general knowledge of the paper, abstract confirms six arcs only.
license: CC BY 4.0 (EPJ Data Science, open access)

title: All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect
authors: Balca Alaybek, Reeshad Dalal, et al.
key_findings: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 170:104149. 174 effect sizes; peak-end effect on retrospective evaluations large (r = .581, 95% CI .487-.661), robust across tested boundary conditions.
Peak-end effect about as strong as the overall average of the experience, and stronger than trend and variability effects.
practical_applications: Design one clear peak and a deliberate ending; but do not ignore the average — the whole piece must be decent.
limitations: Search summary; peak-end not a replacement for average; day-long experiences may not follow it (secondary).

title: Patterns of Affective Reactions to Advertisements: The Integration of Moment-to-Moment Responses into Overall Judgments
authors: Hans Baumgartner, Mita Sujan, Dan Padgett
key_findings: Overall ad judgments driven mainly by the peak emotional moment and the final moment, plus how fast moment-to-moment reactions improved (trend).
Duration only weakly related to overall judgments; longer ads have an advantage if they build toward a peak.
Adaptation may explain preference for delayed peaks and high endings; longer ads can both raise and lower liking.
practical_applications: In ads/clips put the peak late-ish and end high; an upward trend helps; extra length only if it builds.
limitations: Abstract-level; 1990s TV ads; journal (Journal of Marketing Research) from general knowledge, not confirmed in snippet.

title: Affective Forecasting: Knowing What to Want
authors: Timothy D. Wilson, Daniel T. Gilbert
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 14(3):131-134. Impact bias: people overestimate intensity and duration of future emotional reactions.
Causes: focalism (attending to one aspect of the future), immune neglect, failure to anticipate how quickly they will make sense of events (speeding recovery).
practical_applications: Creators over-predict how strongly an audience will feel a moment: test with real viewers; brief negative beats fade faster than feared, so audiences recover — but do not rely on predicted 'wow'.
limitations: Abstract/excerpts; about life events, applied to media by analogy (DERIVED).

title: Mood management through communication choices
key_findings: American Behavioral Scientist 31(3):327-341 (per secondary). People select media to regulate mood: bored people choose exciting content, stressed people calming content.
Content dimensions: excitatory potential, absorption potential, semantic affinity, hedonic valence (fourth dimension named in other secondary sources).
Challenged by the popularity of sad/tragic media (see OliverBartsch2010).
practical_applications: Match the opening energy of a post to the likely state of the viewer (late-night feed = calm), then move them.
limitations: Only secondary sources seen (Wikipedia and reference lists).

title: Appreciation as Audience Response: Exploring Entertainment Gratifications Beyond Hedonism
key_findings: Human Communication Research 36(1):53-81. Three studies develop measures of gratifications beyond fun and suspense: moving and thought-provoking experiences (appreciation).
Appreciation is a response distinct from enjoyment and from emotional valence.
practical_applications: A piece can succeed by being moving/meaningful rather than pleasant; sad-but-meaningful Mint & Tao stories are a legitimate target.
limitations: Abstract-level; film genres.

title: Toward a general psychological model of tension and suspense
key_findings: Domain-general model: tension arises from conflict, instability, dissonance or uncertainty that trigger predictions about emotionally significant future events.
Tension scales with how much the outcome matters, strongest when possible outcomes span very positive to very negative; lack of control adds tension.
Suspense = two clearly opposed outcomes; tension = more diffuse; surprise happens after an event, tension before.
Outcomes can become the next initiating event: chains of tension-resolution at multiple timescales; optimal delay is an open empirical question.
Examples: deceptive cadence delaying resolution, dramatic irony.
practical_applications: Build tension by an open, meaningful question + delayed answer; chain resolutions into new questions for series.
limitations: Hypothesis & theory article; ~70% of page text read; empirical data on delay scarce.

title: Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation
key_findings: ITPRA theory: Imagination, Tension, Prediction, Reaction, Appraisal response systems to expected events; tension linked to uncertainty.
Chapters on creating predictability, surprise and tension.
practical_applications: Music and edit beats: establish predictability before surprise; tension rises before an expected event.
limitations: Publisher/library descriptions only.

title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
authors: Valorie Salimpoor, Mitchel Benovoy, Kevin Larcher, Alain Dagher, Robert Zatorre
key_findings: Nature Neuroscience 14(2):257-262. PET + fMRI: caudate more involved during anticipation, nucleus accumbens during peak emotional experience (chills).
Anticipation of an abstract reward releases dopamine along a pathway distinct from peak pleasure.
practical_applications: Anticipation is itself rewarding: a build-up before a peak (drop, reveal) is part of the pleasure, not dead time.
limitations: Small sample of selected listeners with chills; abstract-level.

title: Emotional responses to music: The need to consider underlying mechanisms
key_findings: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 31:559-621. Six induction mechanisms: brain stem reflex, evaluative conditioning, emotional contagion, visual imagery, episodic memory, musical expectancy; later extended to eight (BRECVEMA, adds rhythmic entrainment and aesthetic judgment).
Commentaries dispute mechanism boundaries and cultural context.
practical_applications: Music cues act through several routes: a sudden loud hit (brain stem reflex) startles regardless of story; a known song triggers memory (nostalgia).
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries.

title: Effects of Musical Tempo and Mode on Arousal, Mood, and Spatial Abilities
key_findings: Music Perception 20(2):151-171. Same Mozart piece in fast/slow and major/minor versions: tempo changed arousal but not mood; mode changed mood but not arousal.
practical_applications: Use tempo as the arousal knob and mode (major/minor) as the valence knob when choosing or briefing music.
limitations: One piece, Western listeners; abstract-level.

title: The role of structure in the musical expression of emotions
key_findings: In Handbook of Music and Emotion (2010) pp. 367-400. Related later chapter by Gabrielsson: tempo, loudness, mode etc. can each signal several emotions; perceived emotion depends on many factors acting together additively or interactively.
practical_applications: No single music parameter = one emotion; brief music by combined profile (tempo + mode + loudness + articulation).
limitations: Bibliographic + abstract of related chapter only.

title: Film Structure and the Emotion System
key_findings: Mood-cue approach: films set a longer-lasting mood that orients viewers; brief emotion cues must recur to sustain the mood; tonal shifts work if the audience is cued to expect them.
practical_applications: Set mood in the first seconds; keep a steady drip of small cues; foreshadow a tonal change before it happens.
limitations: Film-theory (cognitive) book; publisher excerpts and summaries only.

title: Enhancement of experienced sexual arousal in response to erotic stimuli through misattribution of unrelated residual excitation (excitation-transfer test)
authors: Joanne Cantor, Dolf Zillmann, Jennings Bryant
key_findings: Excitation transfer (per secondary): residual arousal from one event intensifies the next emotional reaction, mainly when people cannot attribute the arousal to its real source.
Later study: effect disappeared when people were self-aware of their arousal; an MSU dissertation on TV programs and commercials found no support (assimilation instead).
practical_applications: A high-arousal beat can amplify the beat that follows (e.g. relief/joy after suspense) — keep the gap short; evidence mixed.
limitations: Only Wikipedia/search summaries; title from search listing; mixed replication in media settings.

title: Factors involved in generating suspense
key_findings: Human Communication Research 9:49-58 (per reference list). Snippet (attribution likely, unconfirmed): suspense increased with more positive dispositions toward the protagonist.
practical_applications: Make the audience like the character before putting them in peril; no liking → no suspense.
limitations: Bibliographic; finding attribution unconfirmed.

title: The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation
key_findings: Psychological Bulletin 116(1):75-98. Information-gap theory: curiosity arises when attention focuses on a gap in one's knowledge, producing a feeling of deprivation.
practical_applications: Open a specific, answerable gap in the hook; close it in the body; a vague gap does not pull.
limitations: Secondary/abstract summaries only.

title: Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion
key_findings: Cognition & Emotion 17:297-314. Prototype of awe: perceived vastness + need for accommodation; can be unsettling (not always pleasant).
practical_applications: Awe needs scale (wide shot, small figure) AND something that does not fit existing understanding.
limitations: Theoretical paper; abstract-level. Also in M02 sources.

title: Nostalgia: Past, Present, and Future
authors: Constantine Sedikides, Tim Wildschut, Jamie Arndt, Clay Routledge
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 17(5):304-307. Nostalgia is not only about the past; related work: self-oriented, existential and social functions; ambivalent but more positive than negative; supports meaning via social connectedness; future-oriented (approach, optimism).
practical_applications: Nostalgia beats should end in connection or forward motion, not only loss.
limitations: Snippets of several papers by the same group; full texts not read.

title: Universal Patterns in Color-Emotion Associations Are Further Shaped by Linguistic and Geographic Proximity
key_findings: Psychological Science 31(10):1245-1260. 4,598 participants, 30 nations, 22 languages, 20 emotion concepts × 12 colour terms.
Strong cross-national similarity (mean r = .88) plus nation-specific differences, larger similarity for linguistically/geographically close nations.
practical_applications: Colour-emotion associations are largely shared but locally tuned: check Thai associations; colour terms, not rendered colours, were tested.
limitations: Specific colour-emotion pairs not read; colour words not images; Thailand participation not confirmed.

title: Attention and the evolution of Hollywood film
authors: James E. Cutting, Jordan E. DeLong, Christine E. Nothelfer
key_findings: Psychological Science. 150 popular films 1935-2005: shot-length sequences increasingly approximate 1/f patterns; average shot length fell (press: ~8-10 s in 1960s to ~3-4 s by 2005); variation pattern independent of mean.
practical_applications: Vary shot lengths in a structured way (clusters of short shots, then longer holds) rather than uniform cuts.
limitations: Secondary coverage; ASL as a measure criticised.

title: The evolution of pace in popular movies
key_findings: Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. 180 films 1930-2015: shot duration, motion and luminance across film structure; snippet: altered patterns affect pace, with increasing shot durations and decreasing motion in the setup.
practical_applications: Openings (setup) can be slower and calmer; pace increases toward climaxes (DERIVED from pattern).
limitations: Snippet only; feature films, not short social video.

title: (Camera angle and product evaluation in advertising, 1992)
key_findings: As cited by Schuldt, Konrath & Schwarz 2012: products photographed from a low camera angle were evaluated more positively than from high or eye level.
Twente thesis (2009): moderation by need for cognition not reproduced; camera-angle effect significant for faces but only one of six objects.
practical_applications: Low angle = more power/positivity is a weak, fragile effect; treat as CRAFT-plus, not law.
limitations: Original paper not seen; title/journal unconfirmed; partial replication failure.

title: Emotional Contagion
authors: Elaine Hatfield, John T. Cacioppo, Richard L. Rapson
key_findings: Current Directions in Psychological Science 2(3). Automatic mimicry of expressions, voices, postures → feedback → emotions converge (per secondary summaries). Covered in depth in M02.
practical_applications: The on-screen character's/narrator's emotion is the lowest-level route to the viewer's.
limitations: Bibliographic; see M02 (Hatfield1993, ManySmiles2022) for evidence strength.

title: How does an editor control the rhythm of a film
key_findings: Practitioner guide on edit rhythm (pace via shot length, cutting on action/beat, holding shots for emotion).
practical_applications: Craft reference for edit-rhythm cells in the matrix.
limitations: Tier D, only search listing seen.
